To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in a random sample of men aged 45 to 75, edentulous subjects were more likely to have coronary heart disease (prevalence 19.8%) than dentate subjects were (12.1%).
edentulousness, and serological markers of periodontitis, are associated with CHD in middle-aged men.
the prevalence of coronary heart disease was higher in subjects with a positive serological response to periodontal pathogens than those with a negative response.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between periodontal disease and atherosclerosis.
the association of coronary atherosclerotic disease with the presence of serum antibodies against periodontal pathogens and the presence of periodontal disease.
the role of oral infections in cardiovascular disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the association of CHD and periodontal infection is still uncertain.
the association between antibodies and CHD is not a causal one.
periodontal disease is a risk factor of atherogenesis and cardiovascular disease, and it may be a modifiable risk factor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of antibodies against periodontal pathogens is associated with coronary heart disease.
periodontal pathogens may contribute to the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, and the host’s response to periodontal pathogens is associated with the severity of atherosclerosis.
periodontitis is associated with coronary artery disease, but the association is not causal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
periodontal disease may be a risk factor for coronary heart disease.
the presence of periodontal infection may be a risk factor for CHD.
periodontitis may be associated with CHD and that this association is mediated by the immune response to periodontal infection.
